extracted.intended_audience: students training for math competitions / olympiads (high-school to early undergraduate)
extracted.subtask_description: Solving and proving results in elementary number theory and enumerative combinatorics with emphasis on competition-style problems and standard techniques (Euclidean algorithm, congruences, PIE, combinatorial bijections, descent, factorization, Pell equation, Beatty sequences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Solve linear recurrences by characteristic equation
rubrics_metrics.description: For linear homogeneous recurrences (e.g., xn+1 = 2 xn + xn−1) form the characteristic polynomial (λ^2 = 2λ + 1), find its roots λ1, λ2 and write xn as a closed-form combination of λ1^n and λ2^n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute characteristic equation, find roots (possibly 1 ± √2 etc.), then determine constants from initial conditions. Examples in the text show eliminating auxiliary variables (like yn) to obtain a single recurrence for xn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find top-ranked elements in knockout tournaments with minimal comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: To find the heaviest (rank 1) of 128 objects using pairwise comparisons requires 127 comparisons (single-elimination). Candidates for rank 2 are those who lost to rank 1 (seven objects), which can be resolved in at most 6 additional comparisons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General strategy: run single-elimination to find winner, then run an elimination among the sequence of direct losers to the winner. Gives total 127 + 6 = 133 comparisons for rank 1 and 2; for ranks 1–3 the text gives reasoning to get at most 139 comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lower bound necessity for comparisons in knockout selection
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine the top object among N by pairwise comparisons requires at least N−1 comparisons because every non-winning object must lose at least once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: shows 127 comparisons are necessary for 128 objects and exhibits constructions where 127 suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use PIE (Principle of Inclusion–Exclusion) for combinatorial estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the inclusion–exclusion principle to count or bound set sizes (e.g., counting maximal double-free subsets, estimating f(n) via alternating series n − n/2 + n/4 − n/8 + ...).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text gives explicit alternating series and refers to using PIE to obtain necessary estimates; mentions harder problems where PIE is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Average minimum element of r-subsets equals (n+1)/(r+1)
rubrics_metrics.description: The arithmetic mean of the least elements of all r-element subsets of {1,...,n} equals (n+1)/(r+1). More generally, the mean of the k-th largest elements is k(n+1)/(r+1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple proofs provided: bijection counting (strip smallest element from (r+1)-subsets), bipartite graph degree-average argument, and a probability/circle symmetry argument choosing r+1 points on (n+1)-cycle and using expected gap length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bound on codewords with Hamming distance ≥ 3
rubrics_metrics.description: If p binary words of length n differ pairwise in at least three positions (distance ≥ 3), then p ≤ 2^n/(n+1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct columns listing words at Hamming distance exactly one from each word; using that there are at most 2^n binary words gives p(n+1) ≤ 2^n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting permutations with forbidden adjacent pairs via PIE
rubrics_metrics.description: To count permutations avoiding certain adjacencies (pleasant permutations), set up sets Ak for each forbidden adjacency and apply the PIE to bound |A|; the alternating series gives asymptotic fraction 1−e^{−1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute |Ak| and intersections |Ak∩Al| via factorial counts and derive bounds like |A| > (2n)!/2 and limit |A|/(2n)! → 1 − e^{−1}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting nonrepeating binary n-words via recurrence and cyclic shifts
rubrics_metrics.description: An n-word is repeating if it is d | n copies of a shorter block. The recurrence counting nonrepeating words arises from subtracting repeating patterns; cyclic shifts of a nonrepeating block produce n distinct nonrepeating n-words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use structure of nonrepeating initial block and cyclic shifting to count nonrepeating words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parking functions count (relation to Cayley's theorem)
rubrics_metrics.description: Number of good preference sequences in a parking problem equals (n+1)^{n−1}. By adding an (n+1)-st lot and considering cyclic shifts of (n+1)^n sequences, exactly one shift per orbit is good, giving (n+1)^{n−1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This combinatorial argument extends to a proof of Cayley's theorem on labeled trees (n^{n−2} forms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: divisibility notation
rubrics_metrics.description: a | b denotes that a divides b (equivalently b = a q for some integer q).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Basic notation used throughout; used in subsequent theorems and problem statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental properties of divisibility
rubrics_metrics.description: I. a|b and b|c ⇒ a|c. II. If d|a and d|b then d|ax + by (hence d|a+b, d|a−b). III. If any two of a, b, c are divisible by d in a + b + c, then the third is divisible by d.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard closure properties; used for linear combinations and modular reasoning in many problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division algorithm (existence and uniqueness of quotient and remainder)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every integer a can be uniquely written as a = b q + r with integer q and 0 ≤ r < b (for positive b); q and r are quotient and remainder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foundation for modular arithmetic and Euclidean algorithm.

rubrics_metrics.name: GCD properties and Euclidean algorithm (including representation)
rubrics_metrics.description: gcd(a, b) basic values (gcd(a,1)=1, gcd(a,a)=a, gcd(a,0)=a) and gcd(a,b)=gcd(b,a−b). Division identity a = bq + r ⇒ gcd(a,b) = gcd(b,r). Also gcd(a,b) can be represented as ax + by for integers x,y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives algorithmic method for computing gcd and the Bezout identity; special case: if gcd(a,b)=1 then ax+by=1 has integer solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation gcd·lcm = a·b
rubrics_metrics.description: gcd(a,b) · lcm(a,b) = a · b.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful in multiplicative counting and reasoning about divisibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of prime
rubrics_metrics.description: A positive integer is prime if it has exactly two divisors (1 and itself).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in all prime-related theorems and lemmas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Euclid's lemma
rubrics_metrics.description: If p is prime and p | a b then p | a or p | b.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fundamental for unique prime factorization and many number-theoretic proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
rubrics_metrics.description: Every positive integer has a unique representation as a product of primes (up to order).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in proofs about primes, multiplicities, and factorization-based arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinitely many primes via factorial construction
rubrics_metrics.description: There are infinitely many primes because for any n, any prime p ≤ n divides n! + 1 is false, so new prime divisors must exist (standard Euclid argument using n! + 1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also shows sequences n!+2, ..., n!+n produce consecutive composites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bound on smallest prime factor
rubrics_metrics.description: The smallest prime factor of a composite n is ≤ √n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful to limit trial division when searching for factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primes > 3 are of form 6n ± 1
rubrics_metrics.description: All primes greater than 3 are congruent to ±1 modulo 6.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arises from modular considerations mod 6; used to prune possible prime forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parametrization of primitive Pythagorean triples
rubrics_metrics.description: All pairwise-coprime integer solutions to x^2 + y^2 = z^2 are x = |u^2 − v^2|, y = 2 u v, z = u^2 + v^2 with gcd(u,v)=1 and u, v of opposite parity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard parametrization used to generate and classify Pythagorean triples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congruences and basic modular arithmetic rules
rubrics_metrics.description: a ≡ b (mod m) ⇔ m | a − b; congruences can be added, subtracted, multiplied; ak ≡ bk (mod m) and f(a) ≡ f(b) (mod m) for integer polynomials f; cancellation: if gcd(c,m)=1 and ca ≡ cb (mod m) then a ≡ b (mod m).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists consequences like polynomial substitution and cancellation under coprimality; necessary caution about dividing when gcd ≠ 1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fermat's Little Theorem (and three proofs)
rubrics_metrics.description: For prime p and integer a: a^p ≡ a (mod p); if gcd(a,p)=1 then a^{p−1} ≡ 1 (mod p).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three proofs presented: (1) induction using binomial coefficients, (2) multiplicative permutation of residues 1a,2a,...,(p−1)a and cancellation of (p−1)!, (3) combinatorial necklace-counting showing (a^p − a) divisible by p. Also mention of the cancellation rule to deduce a^{p−1} ≡ 1 when gcd(a,p)=1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fermat converse false (Carmichael-type counterexample)
rubrics_metrics.description: The congruence a^p ≡ a (mod p) does not imply p is prime; example: 341 divides 2^{341} − 2 but 341 = 11·31 is composite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warns against using FLT converse as primality test; gives explicit counterexample and sketch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Euler's theorem (generalization of Fermat)
rubrics_metrics.description: If gcd(a,m)=1 then a^{φ(m)} ≡ 1 (mod m), where φ(m) is Euler's totient function counting integers ≤ m and coprime to m.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard generalization used for modular exponent reductions modulo composite m.

rubrics_metrics.name: Floor function identities and properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Properties: (a) floor(x + y) ≥ floor x + floor y with equality iff fractional parts add < 1; (b) floor(floor(x)/n) = floor(x/n); (c) floor(x + 1/2) gives nearest integer with tie conventions; (d) multiplicity of prime p in n! equals floor(n/p) + floor(n/p^2) + ... .
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful discrete inequalities and counting multiplicities in combinatorics and number theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divisibility identities and Sophie Germain's factorization
rubrics_metrics.description: General facts: a−b divides a^n − b^n; for odd n, a + b divides a^n + b^n. Sophie Germain identity: a^4 + 4 b^4 = (a^2 + 2 b^2 + 2ab)(a^2 + 2 b^2 − 2ab).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these identities to factor seemingly irreducible forms and solve competition problems (e.g., n^4 + 4n composite).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factorization method for proving composite forms (example n^5 + n^4 + 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Find nontrivial polynomial factorization (n^5 + n^4 + 1 = (n^2 + n + 1)(n^3 − n + 1)) by testing roots/symmetries (using ω third roots of unity) or by assuming factor degrees and comparing coefficients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three methods presented: experimentation/table, solving coefficient equations by matching, and using roots of unity to deduce factor n^2+n+1 divides the polynomial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinite descent via parity for Diophantine equations (example x^2+y^2+z^2 = 2xyz)
rubrics_metrics.description: Show only trivial integral solution (0,0,0) by parity: if 2^k divides x,y,z then reduce, deduce contradiction unless all zero, or use infinite descent to force arbitrarily large powers of 2 dividing values, hence only zero solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two solutions shown: parity analysis on highest power of 2 dividing variables and infinite descent repeatedly halving to contradict minimality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive transformations to generate solutions (Pell-type and quadratic forms)
rubrics_metrics.description: When solutions form a closed set under linear transformations (e.g., S and T maps), use them to generate infinite families or to descend to show properties (examples: generating solutions to 2^n = 7x^2 + y^2 or hyperbola x^2 + y^2 − qxy − q = 0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text gives explicit S and T maps, proves they preserve the equation and analyzes parity/monotonicity to conclude existence or to deduce q is a perfect square in certain Diophantine relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of solutions to Pell's equation
rubrics_metrics.description: All integer solutions of x^2 − d y^2 = 1 (d nonsquare positive integer) are given by powers of the fundamental solution x0 + y0√d: (x + y√d) = (x0 + y0√d)^n for n ∈ Z.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses descent: any other positive solution lies between successive powers of the fundamental unit, contradiction. Smallest solution can be found via continued fraction expansion of √d.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beatty sequences complementarity theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: If α and β are irrationals with 1/α + 1/β = 1, then sequences floor(α n) and floor(β n) (n≥1) are disjoint and their union is N (the natural numbers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text gives proof by contradiction using inequalities for αm and βn lying in same integer interval and summing inequalities to get impossibility; note at least one of α,β lies in (1,2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequences missing squares / triangular numbers via floor expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: The sequence floor(n + √n + 1/2) misses exactly the perfect squares; the sequence floor(2n + √(2n) + 1/2) misses exactly triangular numbers. Counting arguments compare ranges to show the omitted set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use inequalities bounding m relative to n to show membership iff m is nonsquare (or nontriangular) and count how many are ≤ a bound to conclude which numbers are omitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solving 1/x + 1/y = 1/p via elementary factorization
rubrics_metrics.description: Set x = p + q, y = p + r to transform into p^2 = q r; when p is prime the only factor pairs give exactly three ordered solutions, otherwise more solutions exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derivation shows x,y > p leads to parameterization; enumerates solutions for p prime: (p+1, p(p+1)), (2p,2p), (p(p+1),p+1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Polynomial congruence property a−b | f(a) − f(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: For polynomial f with integer coefficients, a − b divides f(a) − f(b); use this to derive contradictions (e.g., no integer-coefficient polynomial with f(7)=11 and f(11)=13 since difference 2 not divisible by 4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This divisibility property is a useful short argument for impossibility and injectivity constraints on integer polynomials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Digit/ending arguments for square/non-square identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Use modular constraints and last-digit/last-k-digits analysis (e.g., behavior mod 4, 8, 125) plus digit-position pigeonhole arguments to rule out square possibilities for specially composed numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example problems show eliminating digit patterns and using known divisibility (125, 54) to infer impossibility of square formation.
